cards.statement: BigQuery lets an owner grant BigQuery Data Viewer on a single routine.
cards.explanation: A routine-level grant scopes access to that routine. This supports narrow permissions for users who need to reference it in queries.

cards.statement: BigQuery Data Viewer automatically grants permission to create query jobs in the data's project.
cards.explanation: BigQuery Data Viewer grants data access. Submitting a query also needs permission to create jobs in the execution project, such as through BigQuery Job User.
cards.misconception: Reading table data also grants permission to submit query jobs.

cards.statement: BigQuery lets an administrator relocate an existing dataset by changing its location property.
cards.explanation: BigQuery fixes a dataset's location at creation. Moving its data to another location involves copying or recreating the dataset.
cards.misconception: A dataset's location behaves like an editable configuration property.

cards.statement: BigQuery re-encrypts existing tables when an administrator changes a dataset's default CMEK.
cards.explanation: A BigQuery dataset's default key applies to tables created afterward. Changing that default leaves existing tables' encryption unchanged.
cards.misconception: A dataset default key retroactively changes encryption on its tables.

cards.statement: Pub/Sub can encrypt message attributes with the topic's customer-managed encryption key.
cards.explanation: Pub/Sub applies CMEK at the application layer to message data. Attributes use hardware and infrastructure encryption, so a topic's CMEK excludes them.
cards.misconception: A topic's CMEK covers message attributes as well as message data.

cards.statement: Dataflow can protect persisted Streaming Engine state with a job's customer-managed encryption key.
cards.explanation: Dataflow's CMEK protection includes Streaming Engine state. This keeps persisted streaming state within the pipeline's encryption design.

cards.statement: Cloud Storage requires its service agent to have key-use permissions for CMEK object uploads.
cards.explanation: Cloud Storage's service agent uses the CMEK on the service's behalf. CMEK uploads fail when that agent lacks the required key permissions.

cards.statement: In BigQuery, two AEAD.ENCRYPT calls with the same keyset and plaintext return identical ciphertext.
cards.explanation: AEAD.ENCRYPT picks a new initialization vector on each call, so encrypting one value twice with the same keyset generally yields different ciphertext.
cards.misconception: AEAD.ENCRYPT is deterministic, so equal plaintexts with one keyset give equal ciphertexts.

cards.statement: To re-identify FPE tokens made with a context tweak, Sensitive Data Protection requires that tweak as well as the key.
cards.explanation: Format-preserving encryption (FPE-FFX) is reversible, but tokens created with a context tweak map back to the original values only with the same key and tweak. Cryptographic hashing creates one-way tokens.

cards.statement: Dataform unit tests build their dependency tables by executing upstream workflow actions.
cards.explanation: Dataform unit tests replace an action's dependencies with mock inputs, then compare its SQL result against an expected result set.
cards.misconception: Unit tests execute upstream workflow actions to construct the tested action's inputs.

cards.statement: In Knowledge Catalog, a row-level data quality rule's passing threshold is a maximum number of failing rows.
cards.explanation: A row-level rule's passing threshold is a percentage of rows. Knowledge Catalog fails the rule only when the percentage of rows that pass it falls below that threshold.
cards.misconception: Any violating row fails a Knowledge Catalog row-level rule, regardless of its passing threshold.

cards.statement: Cloud Data Fusion requires a manual output schema update when a hand-edited Wrangler recipe changes the output schema.
cards.explanation: Only recipes created or edited in the Wrangler workspace auto-update the output schema. If a manual recipe edit changes the output, the engineer updates the schema in the Wrangler transformation.

cards.statement: Spanner gives serializable transactions an order consistent with observable real-time commit precedence.
cards.explanation: Spanner's serializable transactions preserve real-time commit order across servers. A transaction that finishes before another starts committing precedes it in that order.

cards.statement: Bigtable commits the mutations across several rows of a batch write as one atomic transaction.
cards.explanation: Bigtable applies batch-write entries atomically per row. A multi-row batch can partly succeed, so applications handle the result for individual entries.
cards.misconception: A multi-row Bigtable batch provides transaction atomicity across the entire batch.

cards.statement: BigQuery can include same-location tables from different projects in one multi-statement transaction.
cards.explanation: A BigQuery transaction commits or rolls back its changes atomically across the participating tables, even when those tables belong to separate projects.

cards.statement: Pub/Sub uses the source topic's dead-letter configuration when a subscriber repeatedly fails a message.
cards.explanation: Pub/Sub stores a dead-letter policy on a subscription. Separate subscriptions attached to the same source topic can use different dead-letter policies.
cards.misconception: Dead-letter handling is configured on a source topic and shared by its subscriptions.

cards.statement: Pub/Sub evaluates exponential retry backoff separately for each message on a subscription.
cards.explanation: Pub/Sub evaluates retry backoff per message after failed delivery. The delay policy addresses transient processing problems at the message level.

cards.statement: Dataflow's exactly-once mode can guarantee a transform's remote calls execute once for each input record.
cards.explanation: Dataflow may rerun a transform after a retry or worker failure. Exactly-once processing deduplicates committed pipeline results, while remote calls can repeat.
cards.misconception: Exactly-once processing guarantees a single invocation of external side effects inside transform code.

cards.statement: In the Apache Beam Java SDK, the Direct Runner checks element immutability and encodability while it runs locally.
cards.explanation: The Java Direct Runner favours correctness over speed and checks that code relies only on semantics the Beam model guarantees, which keeps a pipeline robust across runners such as Dataflow. It is not built for production.

cards.statement: Apache Iceberg managed tables let Apache Spark jobs update the tables by editing their Cloud Storage data files.
cards.explanation: BigQuery manages writes to Apache Iceberg managed tables. Editing their files outside BigQuery can fail consistency checks and cause query failures or data loss.
cards.misconception: An open table format makes direct file edits by external engines safe for BigQuery-managed tables.

cards.statement: The Lakehouse runtime catalog supports Spark, Flink and Trino through the Apache Iceberg REST Catalog API.
cards.explanation: The catalog implements the open source Iceberg REST Catalog API, so open source engines and BigQuery share one set of Iceberg tables without duplicating files.

cards.statement: BigQuery Omni transfers the queried Amazon S3 source files into BigQuery-managed storage before query execution.
cards.explanation: BigQuery Omni runs its query engine where the Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage data resides. Source data stays in the other cloud while BigQuery returns the query results.
cards.misconception: BigQuery Omni imports source files into BigQuery storage before processing them.

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog entry-group access allows a data analyst to read the source data referenced by catalog entries.
cards.explanation: Knowledge Catalog entry-group permissions control access to metadata. Reading the underlying source data needs permissions on the source resource.
cards.misconception: Permission to read catalog metadata also grants permission to read its referenced source data.

source.title: Manage entries and ingest custom sources

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog custom aspects attach structured metadata to individual columns within a catalog entry.
cards.explanation: Knowledge Catalog aspects follow an aspect type's schema and attach to entries or column paths. This lets teams enrich specific fields with business or technical metadata.

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog indexes the descriptions of business glossary terms, so catalog search matches their text.
cards.explanation: A glossary term's description field is indexed for search, and terms link to the data assets they describe, so analysts can find data by its business meaning.

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog discovery scans automatically register Cloud Storage data as BigQuery external or object tables.
cards.explanation: Knowledge Catalog discovery scans infer schemas and group compatible files into external tables. They register unstructured files as object tables, leaving the source data in Cloud Storage.

source.title: Discover and catalog Cloud Storage data

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog search returns a complete asset inventory when engineers filter search to one Google Cloud project.
cards.explanation: Knowledge Catalog search optimizes discovery by returning relevant results. A project filter narrows the search scope but does not guarantee complete inventory coverage.
cards.misconception: Restricting catalog search to one project makes its results exhaustive enough for inventory processing.
cards.volatilityNote: Search recall and inventory retrieval behavior can change as Knowledge Catalog search evolves.

cards.statement: BigQuery Data Transfer Service stages Amazon Redshift migration data in an Amazon S3 bucket.
cards.explanation: BigQuery Data Transfer Service unloads Amazon Redshift data into Amazon S3 before transferring it to BigQuery. The migration design therefore needs staging storage in Amazon S3.

source.title: Migrate schema and data from Amazon Redshift

cards.statement: BigQuery Data Transfer Service skips changed Cloud Storage files after an earlier append transfer loads them.
cards.explanation: In append mode, BigQuery Data Transfer Service reloads a Cloud Storage file when its modification time changes. Rewriting an already transferred file can therefore append its data again.
cards.misconception: A prior successful append transfer permanently marks a file as complete, even after the file changes.

source.title: Load Cloud Storage data into BigQuery

cards.statement: BigQuery Migration Service checks that batch-translated queries match the source SQL's results.
cards.explanation: BigQuery Migration Service performs batch SQL translation on a best-effort basis. Engineers still need to validate the translated queries rather than treating translation success as proof of equivalent results.
cards.misconception: Successful automated SQL translation includes execution-based verification of equivalent query results.

source.title: Migrate code with the batch SQL translator

cards.statement: BigQuery migration assessment uses exported Amazon Redshift table rows to characterize query workloads.
cards.explanation: BigQuery migration assessment analyzes warehouse metadata and query logs. For Amazon Redshift, these inputs describe the schema and workload rather than exporting the tables' business records for assessment.
cards.misconception: Migration assessment infers workload behavior from exported business data instead of metadata and query logs.

cards.statement: Database Migration Service supports destination application writes during continuous source replication.
cards.explanation: Database Migration Service does not support a dual-write migration. Applications keep writing to the source until replication is finalized and the destination becomes a standalone primary.
cards.misconception: Applications can write to the migration destination while Database Migration Service continues replicating source changes.

cards.statement: Database Migration Service lets engineers customize heterogeneous schema conversion with directives.
cards.explanation: Database Migration Service conversion workspaces accept customization directives that override automated conversion rules. Engineers can adapt converted schemas to destination requirements.

cards.statement: Datastream copies historical rows alongside ongoing source changes during initial replication.
cards.explanation: Datastream runs historical backfill and change data capture simultaneously. Large initial datasets therefore do not require waiting for backfill to finish before capturing new changes.

cards.statement: Datastream writes Cloud Storage change events in the order in which the source commits them.
cards.explanation: Datastream does not guarantee event delivery order to Cloud Storage. Downstream consumers use source-specific event metadata to reconstruct the source's sequence of changes.
cards.misconception: The sequence of events arriving in Cloud Storage preserves the source database's commit order.

cards.statement: The Data Validation Tool compares selected-column aggregates between a source warehouse and BigQuery.
cards.explanation: Engineers configure the Data Validation Tool to compare counts, sums, or averages on selected columns. These checks help validate transferred warehouse data against its source.

cards.statement: When all of a key's messages are published in one region, Pub/Sub keeps their order for subscribers in other regions.
cards.explanation: Ordered delivery needs ordering enabled on the subscription and all of a key's messages published in one region. Subscribers can then connect from any region and keep the order.

cards.statement: A Pub/Sub push endpoint acknowledges a message using the HTTP response to the delivery request.
cards.explanation: Pub/Sub interprets accepted response statuses as acknowledgment of the pushed message. The endpoint's HTTP response carries the acknowledgment signal.

cards.statement: Pub/Sub makes messages exported to Cloud Storage readable as soon as it appends them to the output object.
cards.explanation: A Pub/Sub Cloud Storage subscription exposes a message batch after Cloud Storage finalizes its object. Appending a message to an open object precedes that visibility.
cards.misconception: Messages become readable immediately after an append to an export object, before object finalization.

cards.statement: Pub/Sub BigQuery subscriptions can calculate windowed totals across messages before inserting table rows.
cards.explanation: Google recommends Dataflow when Pub/Sub ingestion needs windowing or aggregation across messages. BigQuery subscription transforms modify individual messages.
cards.misconception: A BigQuery export subscription performs cross-message windowed aggregation before ingestion.

cards.statement: Pub/Sub push subscriptions can enable exactly-once delivery for subscriber endpoints in a single region.
cards.explanation: Pub/Sub's exactly-once delivery feature applies to pull subscriptions, including StreamingPull. Locating a push endpoint in one region does not add support for the feature.
cards.misconception: Using one region makes Pub/Sub's exactly-once delivery feature available to push subscriptions.

cards.statement: Pub/Sub timestamp seeks choose messages using the event timestamp supplied by the source application.
cards.explanation: Pub/Sub timestamp seeking uses the publication time recorded by Pub/Sub servers. An application's event time can differ from when its publish request reaches the service.
cards.misconception: Timestamp seeking follows application event time carried in the message.

source.title: Replay and purge messages with seek

cards.statement: Dataflow workers with only internal IPs and Private Google Access reach PyPI through a NAT solution such as Cloud NAT.
cards.explanation: Private Google Access covers Google APIs and services only. Workers with only internal IP addresses reach internet hosts such as PyPI through a NAT solution like Cloud NAT.

source.title: Configure internet access and firewall rules

cards.statement: Dataflow streaming jobs with shuffle on worker VMs need firewall rules that permit traffic between workers.
cards.explanation: When worker VMs perform streaming shuffle, they exchange data through the worker VPC. Firewall rules permitting that peer traffic let the job move records between processing stages.

source.title: Configure internet access and firewall rules

cards.statement: BigQuery deduplicates rows that a client resends to the Storage Write API (gRPC) default stream.
cards.explanation: The Storage Write API (gRPC) default stream uses at-least-once semantics. Exactly-once writes use application-created streams with offsets that identify append positions.
cards.misconception: The Storage Write API (gRPC) default stream deduplicates retried appends.

source.title: Introduction to the Storage Write API (gRPC)

cards.statement: In Apache Beam, once the watermark passes a timestamp, records with earlier event times stop arriving.
cards.explanation: An Apache Beam watermark estimates event-time completeness based on the data source. A record with an earlier timestamp can still arrive later and count as late data.
cards.misconception: Advancing a watermark proves that the corresponding event-time data is complete.

cards.statement: In Apache Beam, a PCollection carries its allowed-lateness setting into downstream derived PCollections.
cards.explanation: Apache Beam propagates allowed lateness to PCollections derived from the configured collection. A later window configuration explicitly overrides that setting when a different tolerance is needed.

cards.statement: Dataflow Streaming Engine moves window state storage from worker VMs into the Dataflow service backend.
cards.explanation: Streaming Engine keeps window state in managed backend infrastructure. Offloading that state reduces worker disk and memory needs and separates state storage from worker replacement.

source.title: Design for flexibility and efficiency on Dataflow

cards.statement: Dataflow FlexRS keeps regular VMs as standby replacements for preempted workers during batch execution.
cards.explanation: FlexRS runs regular and preemptible VMs together during batch execution. The regular workers contribute alongside preemptible workers rather than waiting as standby replacements.
cards.misconception: FlexRS holds regular workers in reserve until preemptible workers stop.

source.title: Use Flexible Resource Scheduling in Cloud Dataflow

cards.statement: Dataflow's at-least-once streaming mode supports BigQueryIO FILE_LOADS for writing records to BigQuery.
cards.explanation: BigQueryIO FILE_LOADS is incompatible with Dataflow's at-least-once streaming mode. For that mode, use STORAGE_API_AT_LEAST_ONCE as the BigQueryIO write method.
cards.misconception: BigQueryIO file loads work with either Dataflow streaming processing mode.
cards.volatilityNote: Supported BigQueryIO write methods can change as Dataflow streaming modes evolve.

cards.statement: With the Pub/Sub AI Inference SMT on a topic, a failing model endpoint makes the publish request fail.
cards.explanation: Google strongly recommends a subscription SMT for AI Inference, so that a throttled or unavailable model leads to retried deliveries instead of failed publishes.

cards.statement: In Apache Beam, ParDo rejects fixed-window side inputs whose window duration differs from its main input.
cards.explanation: Apache Beam projects a main-input window into the side input's window set. The selected side-input window can have a different duration from the main-input window.
cards.misconception: A fixed-window side input needs the same window duration as the main input.

cards.statement: Cloud Data Fusion uses ephemeral Managed Service for Apache Spark clusters for pipeline runs by default.
cards.explanation: The default Cloud Data Fusion compute profile creates a Managed Service for Apache Spark cluster for a pipeline run and deletes it after completion, keeping the cluster lifecycle tied to that run.

source.title: Managed Service for Apache Spark cluster configuration

cards.statement: BigQuery continuous queries can directly use on-demand compute billing for processing incoming rows.
cards.explanation: BigQuery continuous queries use capacity-based compute. They need an Enterprise or Enterprise Plus reservation with a CONTINUOUS assignment.
cards.misconception: Continuous queries share the on-demand compute option used by ordinary BigQuery queries.
cards.volatilityNote: The reservation and edition requirements for continuous queries may change.

cards.statement: Workflows can wait for an external system's HTTP callback before it starts the next pipeline step.
cards.explanation: A Workflows callback endpoint resumes the waiting execution when it receives a request. This coordinates an external completion event instead of repeatedly polling its status.

cards.statement: Classic Dataflow templates can rebuild their pipeline graph from execution parameters at launch.
cards.explanation: Classic Dataflow templates contain a prebuilt static job graph. Runtime parameters supply values to that graph rather than generate a different graph.
cards.misconception: Classic templates construct a new pipeline graph from launch-time parameters.

cards.statement: Dataflow finds a Flex Template's container image through a spec file stored in Cloud Storage.
cards.explanation: A Flex Template packages the pipeline as a container image, usually in Artifact Registry or a private HTTPS registry, plus a JSON spec file in Cloud Storage that points to the image.

source.title: Use Flex Templates to package a Dataflow pipeline for deployment

cards.statement: Dataflow updates worker-count bounds in place for a running streaming job that uses Streaming Engine.
cards.explanation: For Streaming Engine jobs, Dataflow applies minimum and maximum worker updates while the job keeps running with the same job ID.

cards.statement: For a state-preserving update, Dataflow stops the old job when its compatibility check fails.
cards.explanation: For a state-preserving replacement, Dataflow leaves the old job running if the compatibility check fails. It rejects the incompatible replacement.
cards.misconception: An unsuccessful compatibility check stops the original job during a state-preserving update.

cards.statement: Dataflow supports graph-changing replacement updates for a running batch pipeline.
cards.explanation: Dataflow's pipeline update feature applies to running streaming jobs. Engineers run changed batch pipeline code as another job.
cards.misconception: Dataflow's streaming replacement mechanism also updates running batch pipeline graphs.

cards.statement: Dataform can reach Git repositories in private networks through Developer Connect's proxy.
cards.explanation: Developer Connect's proxy links Dataform to privately hosted Git repositories. Direct HTTPS or SSH connections from Dataform need a public Git endpoint.

source.title: Connect to a third-party Git repository

cards.statement: Dataform release configurations can execute compiled SQL on their compilation schedule.
cards.explanation: A Dataform release configuration's schedule produces compilation results. Workflow configurations schedule execution of those results in BigQuery.
cards.misconception: A scheduled release compilation also executes the compiled SQL workflow.

cards.statement: Dataform uses its default service agent's credentials to run scheduled SQL workflows by default.
cards.explanation: Dataform workflow execution uses a custom service account or user credentials. The default Dataform service agent facilitates execution under the selected identity.
cards.misconception: The default Dataform service agent is the execution identity for scheduled SQL workflows.
cards.volatilityNote: Dataform execution identities and enforced act-as behavior have changed recently.

cards.statement: Bigtable can concentrate sequential writes on one node when row keys begin with timestamps.
cards.explanation: Timestamp prefixes group new writes into a narrow key range, creating a hotspot. A higher-cardinality prefix spreads incoming writes across more of the table.

cards.statement: Bigtable Data Boost can process bulk row deletions using compute isolated from the serving cluster.
cards.explanation: Bigtable Data Boost provides separate serverless compute for analytical reads. It rejects write and delete requests, so bulk deletion needs cluster compute.
cards.misconception: Isolated analytical compute also handles bulk mutations.

cards.statement: Spanner can reduce network traffic for primary-key joins by interleaving child tables with their parent.
cards.explanation: Interleaving places related parent and child rows together in storage. Spanner can perform primary-key joins locally when those rows occupy the same split.

cards.statement: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL replaces a table's row store when its columns enter the columnar engine.
cards.explanation: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL keeps row-based access alongside the column store. Its optimizer can select row-store access even after the table's columns load into the columnar engine.
cards.misconception: Loading columnar data converts the table's underlying storage instead of adding an analytical access path.

cards.statement: Firestore Standard edition supports the Firestore with MongoDB compatibility API for database access.
cards.explanation: The Firestore with MongoDB compatibility API is available in Enterprise edition. Standard edition offers Native mode or Datastore mode, so edition choice determines API compatibility.
cards.misconception: MongoDB compatibility is available in both Firestore editions.
cards.volatilityNote: Firestore edition capabilities and supported access modes can change.

cards.statement: BigQuery rewrites stored data into a new format when a dataset switches to physical storage billing.
cards.explanation: BigQuery changes storage metering when a dataset switches billing models. The stored data keeps the same compressed physical format, so the switch leaves query performance unchanged.
cards.misconception: A storage billing model controls the table's physical representation.

cards.statement: BigQuery bills time travel and fail-safe bytes separately when a dataset uses physical storage billing.
cards.explanation: Physical storage billing charges time travel and fail-safe storage at the active storage rate. Retained historical versions therefore contribute to the dataset's storage bill.

cards.statement: BigQuery starts a daily time partition's expiration interval from the first row inserted into that partition.
cards.explanation: BigQuery calculates a daily time partition's expiration from its midnight UTC boundary. A late-arriving row inherits the partition's age rather than starting a new expiration interval.
cards.misconception: A partition's expiration clock starts when data first arrives.

cards.statement: Cloud Storage postpones an eligible lifecycle deletion while an object hold remains active.
cards.explanation: An object hold blocks the lifecycle Delete action. After the hold is removed, Cloud Storage can delete the object if the lifecycle rule's conditions still apply.

cards.statement: BigQuery can reduce cross-slot shuffling by storing parent-child data in nested and repeated fields.
cards.explanation: Nested and repeated fields keep frequently queried hierarchical data together within execution slots. This reduces the coordination needed to join separate parent and child tables.

cards.statement: BigQuery rejects a row whose integer-range partitioning value falls outside the range defined for the table.
cards.explanation: BigQuery stores rows whose partitioning value lies outside the integer range in the __UNPARTITIONED__ partition. Rows with a NULL partitioning value go to the __NULL__ partition.
cards.misconception: BigQuery rejects rows whose integer-range partitioning value is outside the defined range.

cards.statement: BigQuery can use a scalar subquery reading another table as the constant needed for partition pruning.
cards.explanation: A partition comparison against a value read from another table is dynamic. BigQuery needs a constant filter expression to determine eligible partitions before reading table data.
cards.misconception: A scalar subquery supplies a constant for partition pruning because it returns one value.

cards.statement: BigQuery requires an eligible partition filter when a view reads a table with that requirement.
cards.explanation: A view keeps the base table's partition-filter requirement. The view definition or its calling query needs an eligible predicate for partition elimination.

cards.statement: BigQuery clustering narrows block reads for selective filters on columns containing many distinct values.
cards.explanation: High-cardinality clustering gives BigQuery detailed metadata about where matching values reside. Selective queries use that metadata to skip irrelevant storage blocks.

cards.statement: BigQuery combines cached results with appended rows when it incrementally updates a single-table materialized view.
cards.explanation: Eligible single-table materialized views reuse their stored result after appends to the base table. BigQuery processes the additions and combines them with that result.

cards.statement: BigQuery limits smart tuning to queries that explicitly reference the chosen materialized view.
cards.explanation: Smart tuning rewrites eligible base-table queries to use a matching materialized view. The query author can keep the original base-table references.
cards.misconception: Using a materialized view for acceleration requires rewriting query text to name the view.

cards.statement: BigQuery can use a search index to accelerate equality filters comparing indexed strings with literals.
cards.explanation: Search indexes also serve supported equality predicates on string columns. The optimizer uses the index when it expects a benefit.

cards.statement: BigQuery verifies declared primary-key constraints before using them to eliminate query joins.
cards.explanation: BigQuery trusts declared key constraints during optimization and leaves their enforcement to the data owner. Violating them can produce incorrect query results.
cards.misconception: The optimizer checks actual uniqueness before trusting a declared primary key.

cards.statement: BigLake tables use a connection's service account to read the external files queried by a user.
cards.explanation: A BigLake table delegates external file access to its connection's service account. Query users receive table permissions instead of needing permission to read the underlying files.

cards.statement: BigQuery Storage API connectors bypass a BigLake table's column access policies when Spark reads its data.
cards.explanation: The BigQuery Storage API enforces BigLake table access policies for connector reads. Spark receives data subject to the table's row and column controls.
cards.misconception: Reading through an open-source engine's connector bypasses BigLake table governance.

cards.statement: BigQuery lets a SQL DELETE remove rows from an object table that references Cloud Storage files.
cards.explanation: BigQuery object tables are read-only metadata indexes over Cloud Storage objects. BigQuery rejects DML operations that delete their rows.
cards.misconception: Object table metadata rows support the same SQL deletions as standard BigQuery table rows.

cards.statement: Apache Iceberg managed tables in BigQuery keep their data files in a customer-owned Cloud Storage bucket.
cards.explanation: BigQuery manages Apache Iceberg managed tables while storing their data in customer-owned buckets. This combines managed table operations with customer control of the storage location.

cards.statement: BigQuery automatically tracks new snapshots for an Iceberg external table linked to a JSON metadata file.
cards.explanation: An Iceberg external table created from a JSON metadata file stays tied to that file. Engineers update the table definition to point at newer snapshot metadata.
cards.misconception: A JSON-backed Iceberg external table follows new metadata snapshots automatically.

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog can link custom lineage to catalog entries by matching their fully qualified names.
cards.explanation: Engineers submit custom lineage through the Data Lineage API. Matching fully qualified names connect that lineage to corresponding Knowledge Catalog entries, including entries for on-premises sources.

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog automatically applies an access group's default IAM role to supported data product assets.
cards.explanation: A data product owner assigns a default IAM role to an access group. Knowledge Catalog applies that role across supported assets, reducing per-asset permission configuration.

cards.statement: Knowledge Catalog can group assets from different Google Cloud locations into one data product.
cards.explanation: A Knowledge Catalog data product and its underlying assets reside in the same Google Cloud location. Location therefore constrains which assets a producer packages together.
cards.misconception: A data product groups assets across locations regardless of where those assets reside.
cards.volatilityNote: Data product location restrictions may change as supported assets and governance capabilities expand.

cards.statement: BigQuery can reject an on-demand query before execution when estimated bytes exceed its maximum bytes billed.
cards.explanation: BigQuery checks the estimated bytes against maximum bytes billed before running an on-demand query. Exceeding the threshold fails the query before it incurs a query charge.

cards.statement: BI Engine memory reservations apply to queries running in the reservation's project and location.
cards.explanation: A BI Engine reservation assigns memory to a project in a specific location. Dashboards querying another location need capacity there rather than drawing from the original reservation.

cards.statement: BI Engine can accelerate tables outside its preferred tables list when the reservation has spare memory.
cards.explanation: A BI Engine preferred tables list limits acceleration to that set. Queries against other tables use regular BigQuery slots even when the BI Engine reservation has spare memory.
cards.misconception: Preferred tables receive priority while unused BI Engine memory remains available for other tables.

cards.statement: BigQuery can serve a direct materialized-view query from its last refresh within the max_staleness interval.
cards.explanation: For a direct query, max_staleness permits BigQuery to reuse a materialized view's cached result while its refresh lies within that interval. This trades fresher dashboard data for lower latency.

cards.statement: BigQuery uses an authorized view's grant on the source dataset to read data for the view's consumers.
cards.explanation: The source dataset grants access to the authorized view. Consumers receive access to the view, so it exposes its query result while source-table IAM permissions stay separate.

cards.statement: BigQuery can combine granted row-level access policies by intersecting their filters for the same user.
cards.explanation: BigQuery combines the rows granted by a user's row-level access policies as a union. A row is visible if it satisfies a policy that grants that user access.
cards.misconception: A user covered by multiple row-level access policies sees the intersection of their granted rows.

cards.statement: Inserting rows into a policy-tag-protected BigQuery column requires Fine-Grained Reader on that policy tag.
cards.explanation: Inserts, load jobs and streaming need no fine-grained read access on protected columns. UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE need Fine-Grained Reader, and INSERT SELECT needs it on the queried table.
cards.misconception: Writing into a policy-tag-protected column needs the same Fine-Grained Reader access as reading it.

cards.statement: BigQuery can apply dynamic data masking through a data policy assigned directly to a table column.
cards.explanation: A BigQuery column can reference a data policy carrying its masking rule. That direct assignment removes the need to organize the rule through a policy-tag taxonomy.

cards.statement: Looker stores a persistent derived table inside the Looker instance instead of in the connected database.
cards.explanation: Looker writes a persistent derived table into a scratch schema on the connected database and regenerates it on the schedule you set. The connection needs the Enable PDTs setting turned on.
cards.misconception: Looker keeps persistent derived tables in its own instance storage.

cards.statement: Connected Sheets computes a BigQuery pivot table's aggregates from the rows displayed in its preview.
cards.explanation: Connected Sheets runs pivot-table analysis against the full connected BigQuery data. The sheet's limited preview changes what the user sees in the preview, rather than the source rows used for aggregation.
cards.misconception: The preview row subset is the input for connected pivot-table aggregation.

cards.statement: BigQuery ML automatically reapplies a model's TRANSFORM preprocessing when predicting from new input data.
cards.explanation: A model's TRANSFORM clause preserves its preprocessing pipeline, including learned transformation statistics. BigQuery ML uses the same transformations on prediction inputs.

cards.statement: BigQuery ML automatically standardizes numeric features during boosted tree model training.
cards.explanation: BigQuery ML leaves numeric features unstandardized in its automatic preprocessing for boosted tree models. Tree models are exceptions to the numeric standardization used for many other model types.
cards.misconception: BigQuery ML applies the same automatic numeric standardization to boosted trees as to many other models.

cards.statement: ML.EVALUATE reports training-set metrics by default for a built-in BigQuery ML classifier with a held-out split.
cards.explanation: For a built-in classifier with a held-out split, BigQuery ML evaluates against held-out data. ML.EVALUATE with omitted input returns these saved metrics rather than scoring the fitted training rows.
cards.misconception: ML.EVALUATE's default metrics describe the rows used to fit a classifier even when training reserved a held-out split.

cards.statement: BigQuery ML can automatically reload an imported TensorFlow model when its files in Cloud Storage change.
cards.explanation: BigQuery ML freezes an imported TensorFlow model when it creates the model. Later edits to its Cloud Storage source files leave that imported model unchanged.
cards.misconception: An imported TensorFlow model remains a live link to its source files and refreshes after those files change.

source.title: The CREATE MODEL statement for importing TensorFlow models

cards.statement: Feature Store on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform can use BigQuery tables or views as its offline store.
cards.explanation: Feature values and their history stay in BigQuery tables or views. Feature Store on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform uses these sources instead of provisioning a separate offline data store.
tags: Feature Store on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

source.title: About Feature Store on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

cards.statement: BigQuery ML requires reserved capacity for imported TensorFlow inference on images in object tables.
cards.explanation: Running an imported TensorFlow model against image object tables uses capacity-based pricing through reservations. BigQuery excludes on-demand pricing for this inference path.
cards.volatilityNote: Supported pricing and reservation requirements for object-table inference can change.

source.title: Run inference on image object tables

cards.statement: Google recommends AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING over ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING for new BigQuery embedding queries.
cards.explanation: AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING provides the same functionality as ML.GENERATE_EMBEDDING with simpler output column names. Google's guidance favors AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING for new queries.
cards.volatilityNote: BigQuery AI function names and recommendations change frequently.

cards.statement: With a vector index in use, BigQuery VECTOR_SEARCH returns the exact nearest neighbors.
cards.explanation: VECTOR_SEARCH uses approximate nearest neighbor search when it uses a vector index. Searching fewer candidates trades recall for speed, so it can miss an exact nearest neighbor.
cards.misconception: A vector index accelerates VECTOR_SEARCH while guaranteeing the same nearest-neighbor results as an exact search.

cards.statement: BigQuery can automatically refresh a vector index in the background after the indexed table changes.
cards.explanation: BigQuery maintains vector indexes asynchronously as the indexed table changes. New rows can take time to appear in the index because refresh runs in the background.

cards.statement: A BigQuery sharing dataset subscription creates a linked dataset that reads the publisher's tables in place.
cards.explanation: A linked dataset is a read-only pointer to the publisher's shared dataset. Subscribers query its current tables and views from their own project while BigQuery replicates no data.

cards.statement: BigQuery sharing egress restrictions let a publisher block subscribers from copying or exporting linked dataset tables.
cards.explanation: With data egress restricted on a listing, copy, clone, export and snapshot operations are unavailable, and so are writes to destination tables. Publishers can also restrict query results.

cards.statement: BigQuery sharing lets a publisher delete a Pub/Sub topic listing while its linked subscriptions remain active.
cards.explanation: A listing with a shared Pub/Sub topic and active subscriptions cannot be deleted. The publisher first revokes them, which detaches each linked Pub/Sub subscription from the shared topic.
cards.misconception: Deleting a shared topic listing cleans up its active subscriber subscriptions automatically.

cards.statement: Cloud Marketplace orders decide whether a buyer keeps access to a Marketplace-integrated BigQuery sharing listing.
cards.explanation: Subscribing places a linked resource in the buyer's project, and an active Cloud Marketplace order keeps it accessible. Publishers can still add subscribers manually, outside Marketplace transactions.

source.title: Commercialize listings on Google Cloud Marketplace

cards.statement: BigQuery rejects an aggregation threshold query in a data clean room when one result group has too few privacy units.
cards.explanation: Under the aggregation threshold analysis rule, BigQuery omits groups whose distinct privacy unit count falls below the threshold. The query still returns the groups that meet it.
cards.misconception: A single group under the threshold makes the whole aggregation query fail.

source.title: Restrict data access using analysis rules

cards.statement: BigQuery query templates hide the template's routine definition from data clean room subscribers.
cards.explanation: Query templates share approved table-valued functions. Subscribers run only the approved queries and see the table input parameter, while the routine definition stays hidden.

cards.statement: A BigQuery authorized dataset gives views created in it later access to the shared dataset's tables.
cards.explanation: Authorizing a dataset covers its current and future views. A user who can query a view in that dataset reads the shared tables through it without access to the shared dataset.

cards.statement: Data Studio connects a BigQuery data source with service account credentials from a key file the editor uploads.
cards.explanation: Editors enter only the service account's email. Admins grant the Data Studio Service Agent the Service Account Token Creator role on that account, so no key file is uploaded.
cards.misconception: Data Studio service account credentials work through an uploaded JSON key file.

source.title: Set up a Google Cloud service account for Data Studio

cards.statement: The publishing project pays the query charges when users query a BigQuery public dataset.
cards.explanation: Google pays to store BigQuery public datasets. Each query is billed to the project that runs the job, subject to the monthly on-demand free tier.
cards.misconception: Public dataset queries are billed to the provider rather than to the querying project.

cards.statement: BigQuery capacity-based compute pricing bills each query for the number of bytes that the query processes.
cards.explanation: Capacity pricing charges for compute capacity, measured in slots over time. On-demand pricing is the model that bills the bytes each query processes.
cards.misconception: Both BigQuery compute pricing models meter queries by bytes processed.

cards.statement: BigQuery custom query quotas cap on-demand usage, while queries that run on reservation slots fall outside them.
cards.explanation: Custom quotas limit data processed per day at project or user level, and these query usage quotas apply only to the on-demand pricing model.

cards.statement: A workflow template's cluster selector deletes its chosen Managed Service for Apache Spark cluster after the workflow.
cards.explanation: A cluster selector runs the workflow on an existing cluster that matches its labels, and that cluster persists. A managed cluster is the option that the workflow creates and then deletes.
cards.misconception: Cluster selectors give existing clusters the same ephemeral lifecycle as managed clusters.

source.title: Overview of Managed Service for Apache Spark Workflow Templates

cards.statement: Managed Service for Apache Spark autoscaling adds workers when on-cluster HDFS utilization runs high.
cards.explanation: Autoscaling acts on YARN memory and, by default from image 2.2, YARN cores. Google says it is not intended for scaling on-cluster HDFS, because HDFS utilization is not an autoscaling signal.
cards.misconception: HDFS storage pressure triggers cluster autoscaling.

cards.statement: After Spot preemption, Compute Engine reprovisions a Managed Service for Apache Spark cluster's secondary workers.
cards.explanation: When Spot VMs are preempted, the secondary worker group can run at reduced capacity until Compute Engine reprovisions them. Secondary workers are processing-only and store no data.

source.title: Managed Service for Apache Spark secondary workers

cards.statement: In Managed Airflow, a deferred task keeps its worker slot occupied until the trigger it waits on fires.
cards.explanation: While a deferrable operator waits, a trigger in the environment's triggerer monitors the job and no worker slot is occupied. Deferrable mode needs at least one triggerer.
cards.misconception: Deferring a task still ties up its worker slot.

source.title: Use deferrable operators in Airflow DAGs

cards.statement: In Apache Airflow, the default XCom backend stores the values that tasks push in object storage.
cards.explanation: Airflow's default XCom backend stores values in the Airflow metadata database, so XComs suit small amounts of data. Large values such as dataframes call for another path, such as an object storage backend.
cards.misconception: XComs are stored in object storage by default and suit large payloads.

cards.statement: In Apache Airflow, unpausing a DAG with catchup on creates runs for the intervals missed while it was paused.
cards.explanation: Catchup also triggers when a DAG is turned off for a period and then re-enabled: the scheduler creates a run for each data interval not yet run. Backfill reruns a chosen past period.

cards.statement: BigQuery scheduled queries can authenticate as a service account instead of the user who created them.
cards.explanation: A scheduled query runs with user credentials or as a service account, chosen at creation or updated later. Users signed in with a federated identity need a service account.

cards.statement: A folder's reservation assignment overrides the assignment of a project inside that folder in BigQuery.
cards.explanation: A project uses its single most specific reservation assignment. A project assignment overrides a folder assignment, which overrides an organization assignment.
cards.misconception: Higher levels of the resource hierarchy take precedence over project assignments.

cards.statement: BigQuery charges for a reservation's baseline slots even during periods when no queries use them.
cards.explanation: Baseline slots are always allocated to the reservation and always charged. Autoscaling slots add capacity above the baseline and are charged for the slots scaled up.

cards.statement: BigQuery shares idle slots between reservations in different administration projects of one organization.
cards.explanation: Idle slot capacity stays within one administration project and one region. Reservations in separate administration projects, or in separate organizations, do not share idle slots.
cards.misconception: Idle slots flow freely between all reservations of an organization.

cards.statement: BigQuery lets an administrator create an autoscaling reservation before purchasing any slot commitment.
cards.explanation: Slot commitments are optional for autoscaling reservations. They give a discounted rate for consistently used slots, so buying one is a cost decision rather than a prerequisite.

cards.statement: BigQuery gives a batch-priority query fewer slots than an interactive query once it starts running.
cards.explanation: Batch priority affects queuing: batch queries are more likely to wait when compute is fully used. After a batch query starts, it runs the same as an interactive query.
cards.misconception: Batch priority throttles a query while it executes.

cards.statement: In INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS, a script's parent job reports slot usage that includes its child jobs.
cards.explanation: A multi-statement script job summarizes the values of its child jobs. Slot and cost analyses exclude the SCRIPT statement type to avoid counting total_slot_ms twice.

cards.statement: Dataflow streaming system latency reports the average time that data items have spent processing or waiting.
cards.explanation: System latency is the current maximum time that any data item has been processing or awaiting processing, including time spent waiting inside a source.
cards.misconception: System latency is an average across items rather than the longest wait of any item.

cards.statement: Pub/Sub oldest unacknowledged message age that rises under a small, flat backlog suggests a few unprocessable messages.
cards.explanation: When backlog size stays flat while its oldest unacknowledged message keeps aging, a few messages may be failing processing. Application logs show whether they crash the subscriber code.

cards.statement: Cloud Monitoring meets a metric-threshold condition once most aligned values in its retest window violate the threshold.
cards.explanation: For one time series, every aligned measurement in the retest window must violate the threshold, and a single non-violating value resets the window.
cards.misconception: A majority of violating values within the retest window is enough to meet the condition.

cards.statement: BigQuery adds a job's labels to billing data, so a Cloud Billing export can group on-demand query charges by job label.
cards.explanation: Job labels reach billing data. Dataset labels appear only in storage billing data and table or view labels not at all, so teams label jobs to attribute query costs by team or workload.

cards.statement: With regional placement, Dataflow can ride out a zonal failure by recreating a job's workers in other zones.
cards.explanation: Regional placement picks a zone for each worker at creation across the region's zones. It needs Streaming Engine or Dataflow Shuffle and covers worker VMs, not zonal backend resources.

cards.statement: Dataflow can start a replacement streaming job from a snapshot in a different region from the snapshot.
cards.explanation: Dataflow stores a snapshot in the job's region, and jobs created from it run in that same region. If the snapshot includes Pub/Sub sources, the new job seeks to those Pub/Sub snapshots.
cards.misconception: Dataflow snapshots can move a streaming job to another region.

cards.statement: Pub/Sub can seek a new subscription to a snapshot taken from another subscription on the same topic.
cards.explanation: A snapshot records a subscription's acknowledgment state plus later messages. Seeking another subscription on the topic to it copies that state, for example to replay after a bad deployment.

source.title: Replay and purge messages with seek

cards.statement: Dataset owners query BigQuery fail-safe data themselves once a table's time travel window has ended.
cards.explanation: Fail-safe storage retains deleted data for emergency recovery, but users cannot query or recover it directly. Recovering data from fail-safe goes through Cloud Customer Care.
cards.misconception: Fail-safe extends time travel as another user-queryable window.

source.title: Data retention with time travel and fail-safe

cards.statement: A BigQuery table snapshot keeps a table's data available after the base table's time travel window passes.
cards.explanation: A table snapshot persists until its own expiration, so it keeps a record longer than time travel allows. Snapshots are read-only; restoring one creates a standard table.

cards.statement: BigQuery managed disaster recovery can complete a soft failover while the primary region is offline.
cards.explanation: A soft failover waits until committed changes replicate and needs both regions available. A hard failover promotes the secondary at once, even with the primary offline, and can lose data.
cards.misconception: Soft failover is the option for a primary region that is down.

cards.statement: Bigtable gives read-your-writes consistency on a replicated instance when an app profile uses single-cluster routing.
cards.explanation: Replication between Bigtable clusters is eventually consistent. Sending an application's reads and writes to one cluster gives read-your-writes consistency, while other clusters can lag behind.

cards.statement: Spanner point-in-time recovery reverts an existing database in place to its state at an earlier timestamp.
cards.explanation: To recover a whole Spanner database, engineers back up or export it at a past timestamp within the version retention period, then restore or import it into a new database.
cards.misconception: Point-in-time recovery rewinds the live database itself.

cards.statement: Loading a Managed Airflow snapshot applies the saved scale and networking settings to the target environment.
cards.explanation: Managed Airflow (formerly Cloud Composer) loads configuration overrides, environment variables, PyPI packages, the Airflow database and the dags, data and plugins folders. Scale and networking stay unchanged.
cards.misconception: A snapshot load reproduces the source environment's infrastructure configuration.
